# How to Write a Heartfelt Wedding Speech Using Any AI Assistant

> **In short:** An AI assistant can help you brainstorm, structure and polish a wedding speech, but the heart still has to come from you. Spend 30 minutes feeding it your memories, then rewrite its draft in your own voice before the big day.

Standing up in front of a hundred people with a glass in your hand is nerve-wracking — even when you genuinely love the couple. An AI can't feel the love for you, but it can help you sort your memories into something coherent, find the right words for awkward feelings, and trim the parts that go on too long. This guide works with ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, Le Chat, DeepSeek or any other assistant you already have an account with.

## Before you start
- An account on any AI assistant — the **free tier is fine** for this task; paid plans just give you longer replies.
- **About 30 quiet minutes**, ideally split into two sittings rather than one long block.
- **A rough idea of the couple**: how you know them, how long, a few memories you don't want to forget. You don't need to write anything yet — just have them in your head.

## Step 1 — Collect your raw material first
Before you open any AI tool, sit down for five minutes and write a messy list on paper or in your notes app. Don't worry about sentences — just jot down names, places, inside jokes, the first time you met one of them, a moment that made you laugh, a moment that meant something. The assistant will work better with messy raw material than with a polished paragraph. Think of it as the "ingredients" you lay out before you start cooking — the AI does the sorting, but only if you give it something to sort.

💬 Example: "Met Jess at uni 2015 — she lent me her umbrella in a hailstorm. Tom proposed at the cricket club. They argue about pineapple on pizza. Dad cried at the engagement. Their rescue dog is clearly the favourite child."

You'll know it worked when you have at least 5–8 specific things on your list — places, names, dates, jokes, feelings. If your list has none of those, push yourself to add one more memory before moving on.

## Step 2 — Open any AI assistant and ask it to find your themes
Open the assistant you already use (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, Le Chat — any will do) and start a fresh chat so it doesn't carry baggage from earlier conversations. Paste your messy list into the message box and ask it to spot the patterns, group the stories that go together, and flag the moments worth keeping. Don't ask it to write the speech yet — just to organise your thinking. You're using it like a friend who sorts the photos while you point at the pile.

💬 Example: "Here are some rough notes about my friends Jess and Tom's wedding. Can you spot the themes running through these memories and group them into 3–4 buckets I could build a speech around?"

If you don't see a chat box straight away, look for a button like **"New chat"**, **"Ask me anything"**, or a pencil-and-page icon in the top corner. If the assistant gives a generic reply ("Here are some tips for wedding speeches…"), ignore it and rephrase: "No — I want you to work from MY notes above, not from generic advice."

You'll know it worked when the assistant comes back with 3–4 clear clusters — for example, "how they met", "the funny side", "what they're teaching each other", "the future". If the clusters feel off, push back: tell it which memory doesn't belong where.

## Step 3 — Build a rough outline together
Now ask the assistant to turn those themes into a simple speech outline: an opening line, what to cover in the middle, how to wrap it up. Most wedding speeches land best between 3 and 7 minutes, so ask for a structure that fits that window. Don't accept anything too fancy — a good wedding speech has three beats: a beginning (welcome and your connection to the couple), a middle (the stories), and an end (a wish or toast). Push for a skeleton, not a finished script.

💬 Example: "Using those themes, draft a 5-minute speech outline. I want a warm opening, 2 stories from the middle, and a short, heartfelt closing toast. Keep it simple — bullet points, not full sentences — I'll write the words myself."

If the outline feels too formal or too "corporate", tell the assistant: "Make it warmer, like a friend talking." If it gives you a draft instead of an outline, just reply: "Can you give me bullet points first, no full sentences?" Most tools respond well to that nudge.

You'll know it worked when you have a clear skeleton — three or four beats — that you can read aloud and roughly feel the timing. If you can't imagine standing up and saying it, the outline isn't ready yet.

## Step 4 — Draft in your own voice, sentence by sentence
This is the most important step, and where most people get it wrong. The AI gave you the bones; now **you** write the flesh. Open a blank document and write each section yourself, using the assistant's outline as a guide. Use the words you'd actually say to a friend across a table. When you get stuck on one sentence, copy-paste just that sentence into the chat and ask for 2–3 alternative phrasings — then pick the one that sounds most like you. Never let the assistant write a whole paragraph for you.

💬 Example: "Give me three different ways to say 'I'm so happy for you both' that don't sound like a greeting card. Keep each one short, under 10 words."

If you don't have a word processor handy, the notes app on your phone works just as well — or even the AI chat itself, if you tell it to only ever write one sentence at a time. The rule of thumb: if you couldn't say it at a barbecue, don't say it at a wedding.

You'll know it worked when you can read the whole speech aloud in your normal speaking voice without wincing at any line. If a line makes you cringe on the second read, rewrite it before moving on.

## Step 5 — Ask the AI to tighten and check
Now that you have a real first draft, paste it back in and ask for two specific things: where it drags on too long, and any lines that sound generic. Most assistants are good at this — they're excellent at cutting. Be specific about the length you want and **don't ask it to "make it better"** — vague instructions give vague results. Keep your voice in charge.

💬 Example: "Here's my draft. It needs to fit 5 minutes. Flag any sentences that sound generic or cliché, and point out spots where I'm repeating myself. Don't rewrite anything — just point out the weak spots and explain why."

If the assistant rewrites whole sections, that's a sign you asked too broadly. Try again with: "Just bullet points, no rewrites." If the draft is way too short, ask instead: "Where could I add one more concrete detail?" — not "Write more." The AI cannot create a memory you didn't have, and you'll always hear the seams when it tries.

You'll know it worked when you have a tight draft you can read in roughly the right time, with your own voice still clearly there. If the result sounds like it could come from any wedding, anywhere, push back harder.

## Step 6 — Read it out loud, twice, and tweak
Close the laptop and read the speech out loud — to yourself, to a mirror, to a patient housemate, to the dog. Mark every spot where you stumble, run out of breath, or laugh involuntarily; those are the lines to fix. Then read it once more standing up, with a glass of water in your hand, the way you will on the day. Time yourself so you know what 5 minutes actually feels like. This is where the AI stops helping and you take over.

💬 Example: "Read it aloud once for flow, once for timing, and write down the seconds where you hesitated or lost your place."

If you live alone and want a listener, use a voice recorder app on your phone — or send the draft to a friend and ask them to read it back to you over a call. A speech that works on paper can feel slow when spoken, and vice versa. Trust the read-aloud test more than any prompt.

You'll know it worked when you can deliver the whole speech once, out loud, in roughly 5 minutes, and feel okay doing it. A little nervous is fine. Terrified is a sign you need one more pass — usually a shorter one.

## Common mistakes
- **Letting the AI write the whole speech in one go.** The result will sound polished and empty. Keep it as a thinking partner, not a ghostwriter — the couple wants *your* voice, not a generic one.

- **Forgetting to add a name, a date, a place.** The AI doesn't know your friend said something hilarious at their own engagement party — only you do. Specifics are what make a wedding speech land. If your draft has no proper nouns, it isn't finished.

- **Writing too long.** Three minutes is plenty for most weddings. If the AI gave you ten minutes of material, the cure is always cutting, not adding. A short, tight speech beats a long, wandering one every time.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** This same "raw material → outline → draft in your own voice → trim" pattern works for any writing you actually care about — birthday cards, retirement speeches, thank-you notes, even tricky emails. The AI does the sorting; you do the caring.

- **For your business or work:** The skill here is *using the tool as a thinking partner, not as a writer*. That's the same rule for emails, reports, anything where your name goes on the finished product. People can tell the difference.

- **If you're just getting started:** Don't try half a dozen different AI tools for this. Pick the one you already have an account with and stick with it. The best assistant is the one you'll actually open — the model matters far less than your own memories do.

## Try it now
Open your AI assistant right now and paste in three sentences about the couple — even just "met in 2018, she's a teacher, he can't cook, they got a rescue dog last year." Then ask: **"What are the stories hiding in this?"** That's the whole starting point. Twenty minutes from now you'll have an outline.
